tytul: Cornelian cherry jam (processed as NCHFP describes)
wstep: This card describes a cornelian cherry jam without added pectin from the bylena.com recipe: cornelian cherries simmered in water, pressed through a sieve and cooked with the same weight of sugar, filled into sterile jars and processed in a boiling-water bath as NCHFP describes for jam without added pectin.

ostrzezenia.tekst: Store sealed jars in a cool, dark, dry place at 50–70 °F (about 10–21 °C) and, for best quality, use them within a year: NCHFP gives up to a year of best quality for jams and jellies made from a tested recipe and processed for the recommended time, and this card is not a tested recipe.
Do not reduce the sugar: NCHFP warns that in traditional recipes too little sugar prevents gelling and may allow yeasts and molds to grow.

sekcje.naglowek: About the fruit and the recipe
akapity: Cornelian cherries are acidic fruit: selected genotypes from Turkey had a pH of 2.87–3.12 (3-year means), and fruit from another population a pH of 2.60–4.02.
Because fruit acidity varies, this card does not promise any particular pH for the jam; it relies on the full amount of sugar and on the NCHFP filling and processing rule.

The bylena.com recipe is not a tested canning recipe: it pours the jam into clean, dry jars and gives no boiling-water bath or headspace; JarAtlas does not skip them and takes them from the NCHFP rule for jam without added pectin.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): make the jam only from cornelian cherries, water and sugar in the proportions below, without other fruit or spices.
According to the bylena.com recipe, the jam uses 2 kg of cornelian cherries, enough water to cover them, and sugar equal in weight to the sieved purée (about 1 kg of purée to 1 kg of sugar).
NCHFP warns not to reduce the sugar in traditional recipes: too little sugar prevents gelling and may allow yeasts and molds to grow.
NCHFP fills jam without added pectin into sterile jars; JarAtlas uses sterile jars at every elevation.
NCHFP puts the empty jars right side up on the rack in a boiling-water canner and fills the canner and jars with hot (not boiling) water to 1 inch (about 2.5 cm) above the tops of the jars.
To sterilize empty jars, NCHFP boils them for 10 minutes below 1000 ft, and above that 1 minute longer for each additional thousand feet.
JarAtlas rule for metres: boil the jars for 10 minutes up to 300 m, and add 1 minute for every further 300 m or part of it.
Cover the cornelian cherries with water, bring to the boil, then turn the heat to low and simmer for 30 minutes.
Press the fruit through a sieve to remove the pits, and weigh the purée.
Add the same weight of sugar, bring to the boil and simmer on low heat for 1 hour, stirring from time to time.
Just before filling, remove and drain the hot sterilized jars one at a time.
Fill the hot jam into the sterile jars, leaving 1/4 inch (about 0.6 cm) of headspace, seal them with self-sealing two-piece lids and process them in a boiling-water canner.

Keep the water at least 1 inch (about 2.5 cm) above the jar tops during processing, and 2 inches (about 5 cm) above the jars if the processing time is over 30 minutes; if needed, add boiling water around the jars, not onto them.
Start timing only once the water is boiling.
Do not seal the jars with paraffin or wax: NCHFP no longer recommends paraffin or wax seals for any sweet spread, because of possible mold contamination.
Up to 1000 ft (up to 300 m) process half-pint and pint jars for 5 minutes.
Above 1000 ft the food may spoil if the time is not increased.
Above 1000 ft (above 300 m) process them for 10 minutes, and above 6000 ft (above 1800 m) for 15 minutes.
The card converts feet to metres and rounds the limits down, towards the longer time: 1000 ft becomes 300 m and 6000 ft becomes 1800 m.
Shortening the time or cooling jars in cold water can also lead to spoilage.

When the time is up, turn off the heat, remove the canner lid and wait 5 minutes before taking the jars out; NCHFP says this wait is not needed for food safety when USDA or University of Georgia times are used.
The NCHFP table gives times only for half-pint and pint jars.
JarAtlas rule (cautious; the NCHFP table stops at pints): a pint holds about 473 ml, so a 0.5 l jar has no tested time in this recipe; use jars of up to 473 ml.
When you take the hot jars out of the canner, do not retighten the lids or bands; this can cut through the gasket and cause seal failures.

Cool the jars at room temperature for 12 to 24 hours, then remove only the screw bands (the metal rings of two-piece lids), leaving the flat lids on the jars, and test the seal: press the middle of the lid, and if it springs up when you release it, the jar is not sealed.

NCHFP calls Mason-type canning jars with self-sealing two-piece lids (a flat lid and a screw band) the best choice, and this seal test and the method on this card assume them; NCHFP does not recommend other commercial jars whose mouths cannot be sealed with two-piece canning lids for canning any food at home.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): use this card only with jars that take two-piece canning lids; it gives no method for twist-off jars or jars with glass lids, so do not use them for this recipe.
A sealed lid is concave, curved down slightly in the centre; if the centre is flat or bulging, the jar may not be sealed.
If a jar has not sealed at this check, keep it in the refrigerator and eat it within several days.

Store sealed jars in a clean, cool, dark, dry place, not above 95 °F (35 °C) and not near hot pipes, a stove or a furnace, in an uninsulated attic or in direct sunlight; in such conditions the food may spoil.
Keep opened jam in the refrigerator at 40 °F (about 4 °C) or lower.
JarAtlas rule: keep an opened jar in the refrigerator and use it within 1 month, the time NCHFP gives for regular full-sugar cooked jams.
Opening the jar often or leaving it out at room temperature for long periods shortens this time; you can spoon the amount you need into a bowl and put the jar back in the refrigerator quickly.
Keep the opened jar in the refrigerator until it is used up.
Before using a stored jar, check that the lid is tight and holds a vacuum: a good seal has a concave centre.
Look for streaks of dried food running from the top of the jar, rising air bubbles and unnatural colour.
When opening the jar, check for an unnatural smell, spurting liquid and cotton-like mould on the food or under the lid.
Do not taste food from a jar with an unsealed lid or with signs of spoilage.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): throw out such a jar.
Discard jam with mold on it; USDA and microbiologists advise against scooping out the mold and eating the rest.
Check an opened jar regularly for signs of spoilage such as mold, yeast or an off odor, including a fermented, yeasty or alcohol smell; if you find any, throw out the whole jar.
